qs.q: Amount of dietary iodine in the control of thyroid hormone secretion
o: Low iodine intake stimulates TSH production, leading to increased thyroid hormone synthesis and goiter.
High iodine intake directly stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis.
Iodine is a cofactor for T3 and T4 degradation.
Iodine is a substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis.
qs.e: Iodine is an essential component of thyroid hormones (thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3)). The thyroid gland actively transports iodine from the blood to synthesize these hormones. A deficiency in dietary iodine leads to impaired thyroid hormone production, which in turn stimulates the pituitary gland to release more TSH, leading to thyroid enlargement (goiter) in an attempt to capture more iodine. qs.q: Regarding the control of thyroid hormone secretion, which of the following statements about dietary iodine is true?
o: Excess iodine directly raises TSH release
Both iodine shortage and surplus may disrupt thyroid function
Insufficient iodine directly blocks thyroid hormone production
Iodine is mainly accumulated in the adrenal glands
qs.e: Adequate dietary iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. Both iodine deficiency (leading to goiter and hypothyroidism) and excessive iodine intake (e.g., Wolff-Chaikoff effect, Jod-Basedow phenomenon) can disrupt thyroid function.

qs.q: Growth hormone secretion is increased by all except ---
o: Pharmacologic hydrocortisone (It suppresses GH when used pharmacologically.)
qs.e: Pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids like hydrocortisone suppress growth hormone secretion.

qs.q: Excess growth hormone secretion before epiphyseal closure most characteristically causes
qs.e: Excess GH before epiphyseal plates close stimulates excessive linear bone growth, producing gigantism. GH can also impair insulin sensitivity, but gigantism is the characteristic growth disorder.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hormone secretion disorders arise when glands release too much or too little hormone, causing systemic effects. Recognizing patterns, triggers, and lab clues guides diagnosis and treatment.

sections.p: Abnormal hormone secretion is defined by hormone levels outside physiologic ranges with corresponding clinical signs. Diagnosis requires a compatible history, physical exam, and confirmatory biochemical testing.
b: Quantitative hormone assay (e.g., serum cortisol, insulin, ADH)
Dynamic tests (e.g., dexamethasone suppression, glucose tolerance) when basal levels are equivocal

sections.p: Severity is graded by hormone concentration, organ damage, and symptom burden. For example, Cushing syndrome uses mild, moderate, severe based on cortisol level and comorbidities.
b: Mild: biochemical abnormality, few symptoms
Moderate: biochemical + target‑organ effects (e.g., hypertension)
Severe: life‑threatening complications (e.g., adrenal crisis, severe hypoglycaemia)

sections.p: Causes are grouped by glandular pathology, ectopic production, and drug effects. In low‑resource settings, infections and endemic diseases are common triggers.
b: Pituitary adenoma – most common cause of excess prolactin or ACTH
Ectopic neuroendocrine tumour (e.g., small‑cell lung cancer) – SIADH, ectopic ACTH
Infectious granulomas (TB, HIV‑related opportunistic tumours) affecting hypothalamic‑pituitary axis
Medication‑induced (e.g., glucocorticoids, dopamine antagonists)
Autoimmune destruction (e.g., autoimmune thyroiditis) leading to deficiency

sections.p: Patients show syndrome‑specific signs: hyper‑glycaemia and weight loss in excess insulin, hypertension and moon face in cortisol excess, polyuria/polydipsia in ADH excess, or fatigue and cold intolerance in thyroid hormone deficiency.
b: Pattern of symptoms often mirrors the hormone’s normal actions
Acute crises (e.g., adrenal insufficiency) present with shock‑like picture

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm the hormone abnormality, locate the source, and assess end‑organ damage.

t.a: Serum hormone level (e.g., cortisol, TSH, insulin)
t.b: Is the hormone truly elevated or suppressed? High level confirms excess; low confirms deficiency.
Does the gland retain feedback control? Failure to suppress indicates autonomous secretion.

t.a: Imaging (MRI pituitary, CT chest for ectopic tumour)
t.b: Where is the source? Detects adenoma, metastatic lesion, or infection.
Screen for pheochromocytoma when excess catecholamines suspected.

sections.p: Unchecked hormone excess can cause organ failure; deficiency can precipitate crisis.
b: Severe hypertension or electrolyte disturbance in cortisol excess
Hyponatraemia with seizures in SIADH
Adrenal crisis: hypotension, hypoglycaemia, shock

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct hormone levels and support affected organs.
b: Surgical removal of adenoma or ectopic tumour when feasible
Somatostatin analogs (octreotide) to block excess secretion in neuroendocrine tumours
Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) for adrenal insufficiency – mimics physiologic rhythm
Beta‑blockers for catecholamine excess – control tachycardia without worsening hypoglycaemia

sections.p: Regular hormone monitoring, imaging, and assessment of target‑organ function prevent relapse and detect late effects.
b: Quarterly hormone panels for chronic disorders
Bone density scans in long‑standing cortisol excess
Vaccination and infection control in immunosuppressed patients
Cushingoid appearance from obesity vs. true Cushing syndrome
Psychogenic polydipsia vs. SIADH
Thyroiditis vs. primary hypothyroidism
Stress‑induced cortisol rise can mask adrenal insufficiency – repeat test after rest
Biotin supplements cause falsely low TSH – ask about supplements
Hemolysis interferes with insulin assays – repeat with clean sample

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe hypotension or shock (possible adrenal crisis)
Rapidly worsening confusion with hyponatraemia (possible severe SIADH)
Uncontrolled hypertension with hypokalaemia (possible pheochromocytoma or cortisol excess)

faq.q: Why does small‑cell lung cancer cause hormone problems?
faq.a: It originates from neuroendocrine cells that can ectopically produce hormones like ADH or ACTH.
Yes, TB or HIV can infiltrate the pituitary, destroying hormone‑producing cells.

faq.q: When is a dynamic test preferred over a single hormone level?
faq.a: When basal levels are borderline or when you need to assess feedback control.
